s: Allah witnesses every act and records what people do, including what is less or greater than an atom’s weight. Every soul is accountable for its deeds, and nations and individuals are judged fairly.
Punishment includes boiling drink, painful doom, the Fire, disgrace, and the torment of eternity. It comes upon those who disbelieve, deny revelations, do wrong, and persist in rebellion.
Allah’s mercy is given after adversity and is a source of rejoicing for believers. He removes affliction, forgives, and showed mercy to the folk of Jonah (Yunus) when they believed.

l: the resurrection and return to Allah, Surah 10: Jonas (Yunus)
s: All mankind returns to Allah, who brings creation back and judges what people did. The return exposes false inventions, brings remorse to wrongdoers, and establishes the reward or punishment promised by Allah.

Surah 11: Hud presents perfected, expounded Scripture from Allah, calling people to serve Him alone, seek forgiveness, repent, and prepare to return and be raised before Him. It contrasts humble believers who do good works and enter the Garden with disbelievers devoted to worldly life who face the Fire. It then recounts Noah, Hud, Salih, Abraham, Lot, Shu'eyb, and Moses: their peoples reject warnings and commit wrongdoing; Noah and believers are saved in the ship, while the rejecting peoples are destroyed. It closes with Resurrection, worship, repentance, punishment, the Fire, and the Garden.
Scripture perfected and expounded, teaching worship, repentance, resurrection, accountability, and believers’ and disbelievers’ fates.

Allah is the sole deity, Lord, creator of the heavens and earth, and the return of humankind. Wise, informed, mighty, merciful, forgiving, near, and responsive, Allah knows hidden and proclaimed things, hearts, beasts’ habitation, and the Unseen. Allah owns praise and glory, guards all things, determines every matter, provides sustenance and bounty, gives good and strength to those who repent, and can send punishment. The account unfolds from perfected scripture and service to Allah, through messengers, signs, mercy, and the saving of believers, to destruction of wrongdoing peoples and full repayment of every person.
Moses is sent with Allah's revelations and a clear warrant to Pharaoh and his chiefs, while Pharaoh's command leads his people toward the Fire.
Scripture from Allah contains perfected, expounded revelations and challenges claims of invention by calling for ten similar surahs.
Allah's revelations are perfected and expounded; Moses receives them with a clear warrant, while Muhammad is warned not to forsake or feel straitened by what is revealed.
Man is a created being who becomes despairing and thankless when mercy is withdrawn, then exultant and boastful when hardship is removed, except those who persevere and do good works.
The earth, created in six Days, contains beasts dependent on Allah for sustenance; by Allah’s command it swallows water, while disbelievers cannot escape within it.

l: the Day of Resurrection, Surah 11: Hud
s: The Day of Resurrection is a witnessed day after death, when people are raised again and mankind is gathered. Souls speak only by Allah's permission. It ends with the wretched entering the Fire and the glad entering the Garden.

Punishment is an inescapable doom that may be delayed until a reckoned time. When it comes, it cannot be averted and surrounds those who derided it. It befalls people who reject Allah, commit wrongdoing, or follow corrupt commands, through drowning, the awful Cry, raining stones, destruction, and the Fire.

l: the Day of Judgment, Surah 11: Hud
s: The text warns of an awful Day and describes return to Allah and consequences for people's beliefs and deeds.

The Fire is the appointed place and only Hereafter share of disbelievers who desire worldly life and its pomp. It is a watering-place for Pharaoh's people and the destination and abode of the wretched on the Day of Resurrection, where they abide as Allah wills with sighing and wailing.

Believers accept truth from Allah and the Book of Moses, believe, do good works, and humble themselves before their Lord. Few believers accompany Noah and are saved by Allah’s mercy; believers who do good are promised the Garden.

Disbelievers reject truth, revelation, messengers, and signs, calling them invented or magic. They follow false gods or corrupt leaders, invent lies concerning Allah, block His way, and deny the Hereafter. Judged abject by Noah’s folk’s chieftains, they are cursed, tormented, destroyed, and appointed to the Fire as great losers.

l: those who persevere and do good works, Surah 11: Hud
s: Those who persevere and do good works are exempt from despair, thanklessness, exultation, and boastfulness, receiving forgiveness and a great reward.

l: rightful owners of the Garden, Surah 11: Hud
s: Believers do good works and humble themselves before their Lord; they abide permanently in the Garden.

The Garden belongs to those who believe, do good works, and humble themselves before their Lord. It is the destination and abode of the glad on the Day of Resurrection, where they abide as long as Allah wills, receiving an unfailing gift.

The Hereafter is a feared doom and place of full repayment for deeds. Those who seek only worldly life and its pomp, reject Allah’s way, or do wrong face the Fire and are the greatest losers. Believers who do good works and humble themselves before Allah receive the Garden. It is presented as a warning and lesson for those who heed.

Noah is a messenger and plain warner to his folk, serving Allah with clear proof and mercy. He seeks no reward, does not reject believers, builds a ship by Allah’s inspiration, boards it with believers, and later asks about his son before seeking forgiveness.
Noah's folk, led by chieftains with few believers, reject, dispute, and mock Noah; while he builds the ship, their wrongdoing ends in drowning in the Flood.

A ship built by Noah under Allah’s eyes and inspiration carries Noah, believers, his household except those excluded, and male-female pairs of every kind through mountain-like waves; after the water subsides, it rests on Al-Judi.
The Flood begins when the oven gushes water, covers land with mountain-like waves, drowns Noah’s son and disbelievers, then subsides when Allah commands earth and sky.
Noah initially regards his son as household, but Allah says otherwise because of his evil conduct. He refuses the ship, seeks a mountain refuge, and is drowned when a wave separates him from Noah.
Hud, A'ad’s brother and a messenger sent to them, calls his people to serve Allah, seek forgiveness, and repent; trusting Allah, he and believers are saved from harsh doom.
A'ad, Hud's folk, reject Hud's message, deny Allah's revelations, and follow froward potentates; they are destroyed and bear a curse in the world and on the Day of Resurrection.

Salih, a messenger and brother to Thamud, calls them to worship Allah alone, seek forgiveness, and repent. With clear proof, he presents Allah’s camel as a token; after they hamstring it, he warns of a three-day reprieve.
Thamud, Salih's folk, doubts his call and hamstrings Allah's camel token; an awful Cry overtakes them, leaving them prostrate in their dwellings.

l: the camel of Allah, Surah 11: Hud
s: The camel of Allah is given to Thamud as a token to feed in Allah's earth; when Thamud hamstring her, they bring upon themselves threatened punishment.

A prophet who receives Allah's messengers with peace and hospitality, then pleads for the folk of Lot before Allah; mild, imploring, and penitent, he is told the command concerning them has gone forth.
Messengers are sent by Allah to Noah’s folk, bring Abraham good news, then warn Lot of his folk’s destruction, protect him, and instruct him to depart by night.

l: the folk of Lot, Surah 11: Hud
s: commit abominations The folk of Lot practice abominations and reject Lot's appeal to fear Allah. They are overthrown and stones of clay are rained upon them.
Lot, a messenger of Allah, is distressed by the messengers’ arrival and unable to protect them; they tell him to leave by night while his wife remains for destruction.
is_overthrown by Allah [when His command comes to pass] Lot's township is overthrown when Allah's command comes to pass. It is struck by a rain of marked stones of clay.
is_a folk [addressed by Shu'eyb] Midian is warned by Shu'eyb to serve Allah, use full measure and weight, and avoid corruption. Those who do injustice are seized by the awful Cry and destroyed.
Shu'eyb, a messenger sent to Midian, calls for worship, justice in measure and weight, forgiveness, and repentance; he seeks reform, trusts Allah, and is saved with believers when punishment comes.
Pharaoh commands and leads his people; his chiefs follow a command without right guidance. On the Day of Resurrection, he goes before them and leads them to the Fire.
is_due_to Allah [alone] The messengers call their peoples to serve and worship Allah alone. Worship includes establishing prayer and turning away from false gods.

is_required_from people [after asking forgiveness] The messengers urge their peoples to seek Allah's forgiveness and turn to Him repentantly. Allah is described as Merciful, Loving, Nigh, and Responsive to those who repent.

This unit concerns Joseph, his family, and the events through which Allah raises Joseph from the pit and prison to authority in Egypt. Joseph's brethren conspire against him, but he is taken to Egypt, falsely accused, imprisoned, and later released after interpreting the king's dream. Joseph's family eventually comes before him, recognizes him, receives forgiveness, and settles in Egypt. The unit also teaches about Allah's sovereignty, patience, repentance, faith, and the Hereafter.

Joseph sees a dream of eleven planets, the sun, and the moon prostrating before him. His brethren cast him into the pit, and he is sold into Egypt, where he resists temptation, is imprisoned unjustly, interprets dreams, becomes a trusted authority over the storehouses of the land, and is reunited with his family. He forgives his brethren and prays to die muslim unto Allah and be joined to the righteous.

Allah inspires Joseph in the pit, teaches him the interpretation of events, protects him from evil and lewdness, hears his prayer, and grants him power in the land. Allah is described as Knower, Wise, Forgiving, Merciful, the Best of Judges, and the Warden over what people say. Allah's help, mercy, judgment, and punishment are repeatedly affirmed.

Jacob is Joseph's father and is warned not to tell Joseph's brethren about Joseph's dream. He grieves deeply over Joseph and later over Joseph's younger brother, yet maintains comely patience and places his trust in Allah. His sight is restored when Joseph's shirt is laid on his face.

Joseph's brethren resent their father's greater love for Joseph and conspire to kill or cast him away. They throw him into the pit, deceive Jacob, later come to Egypt for provisions, and accuse Joseph's younger brother of theft. They eventually recognize Joseph, admit their sin, and ask forgiveness.

Joseph's younger brother is kept by Jacob until the brethren promise before Allah to return him. Joseph takes him privately into his care, places the drinking-cup in his saddlebag, and uses the resulting accusation to keep him in Egypt. He is later included when Joseph calls his family to come to him.

l: the ruler of Egypt, Surah 12: Joseph (Yusuf)
s: The ruler of Egypt purchases Joseph's household service and later orders Joseph brought before him after hearing of Joseph's interpretation of his dream. He investigates the women’s accusation against Joseph, recognizes Joseph's trustworthiness, and appoints him to authority over the storehouses of the land.

The ruler's wife asks Joseph to commit an evil act, but he refuses and seeks refuge in Allah. Her attempt is exposed when Joseph's shirt is found torn from behind, and she later admits that she asked Joseph for the evil act.

Joseph's cupbearer is one of the two young men imprisoned with Joseph. Joseph interprets his dream as meaning that he will pour wine for his lord, and after his release he eventually remembers Joseph and reports his ability to interpret the king's dream.
Egypt is where Joseph is purchased, where he is established by Allah, and where he later gains authority. Joseph's family eventually enters Egypt safely at his invitation.
Joseph's brethren place Joseph in the depth of the pit after deciding not to kill him. A caravan finds him there, and he is drawn out with a water bucket and hidden as a treasure.

Joseph spends a period in prison after being falsely accused and despite signs of his innocence. There he interprets the dreams of two young men and later explains the king's dream through the report of Joseph's cupbearer.

l: the land of Egypt, Surah 12: Joseph (Yusuf)
s: Allah establishes Joseph in the land of Egypt and gives him authority where he pleases. Joseph becomes responsible for its storehouses and prepares for years of abundance and hardship.

The Qur'an is revealed in Arabic so that people may understand. It narrates the best of narratives, including Joseph's history, and is described as a reminder, a confirmation of existing Scripture, a detailed explanation, guidance, and mercy for believers.
The Scripture is described as verses that make things plain. The Qur'an is presented as a revealed lecture in Arabic and as a confirmation of the existing Scripture.

l: the dream of Joseph, Surah 12: Joseph (Yusuf)
s: Joseph dreams of eleven planets and the sun and the moon prostrating before him. Jacob tells him not to disclose the vision to his brethren, and the dream is later fulfilled when Joseph's family comes before him.

The king dreams of seven fat kine eaten by seven lean kine, and seven green ears of corn alongside seven dry ears. Joseph interprets it as seven years of abundance followed by seven hard years and then a year of plentiful crops.

The famine follows seven years of abundance and consumes much of what has been prepared. Joseph's management of the storehouses enables people, including his brethren, to seek provisions during the hardship.

Joseph is imprisoned after the ruler's wife accuses him, even though evidence shows his innocence. His imprisonment lasts for a time, during which he teaches about Allah and interprets dreams before being brought out with his reputation publicly cleared.

Joseph's brothers' conspiracy begins with their resentment that Joseph and his brother are dearer to Jacob. They plan to kill or cast Joseph away, place him in the pit, and deceive Jacob with false blood on Joseph's shirt.

l: the interpretation of dreams, Surah 12: Joseph (Yusuf)
s: Joseph says that Allah has taught him the interpretation of events and dreams. He interprets the dreams of the two prisoners and the king, providing warnings and guidance about coming events.
The unit teaches that the reward of the Hereafter is better for those who believe and ward off evil. Joseph affirms belief in the Hereafter and asks Allah to join him to the righteous.

Faith in Allah is presented as worship of Allah alone, rejection of partners and false names, trust in Allah's judgment, and hope in His mercy. The unit warns that many people believe in Allah while attributing partners to Him, and calls people to Allah with sure knowledge.

Surah 13: The Thunder (Ar-Ra'd), revealed at Medina, concerns Allah's signs, revelation, guidance, and judgment. It describes Allah's creation and ordering of the heavens, earth, sun, moon, night, day, rain, lightning, and thunder. It contrasts believers and those who disbelieve, describing the rewards of those who answer Allah's call and the punishment awaiting those who reject it. Muhammad is told to proclaim Allah's oneness and his role as a warner, while Allah's knowledge, power, forgiveness, and reckoning are affirmed.

l: Surah 13: The Thunder (Ar-Ra'd), Surah 13: The Thunder (Ar-Ra'd)
s: It is revealed at Medina and presents signs of Allah's power, guidance, revelation, judgment, and the contrasting outcomes of belief and disbelief.

Allah raises the heavens, orders the sun and moon, spreads out the earth, sends water, shows lightning, and causes thunder to hymn His praise. He knows the visible and invisible, guides whom He wills, forgives, punishes, and is the Creator of all things.
Muhammad is addressed as a warner and messenger who recites what Allah has inspired in him. He is commanded to serve Allah alone, reject partners, trust in Him, and proclaim that Allah is his Lord.
The Scripture contains verses revealed from Allah to Muhammad, and what is revealed from his Lord is described as the Truth. Those with knowledge of the Scripture are presented as witnesses.
The earth is spread out with firm hills, flowing streams, neighbouring tracts, vineyards, ploughed lands, and date-palms. Allah reduces its outlying parts and sends water that makes its valleys flow.
Most of mankind do not believe despite the revelation and Allah's signs. Allah is rich in pardon for mankind despite their wrong.
The Fire is the abode of those who disbelieve, who will abide therein.

l: those who disbelieve, Surah 13: The Thunder (Ar-Ra'd)
s: Those who disbelieve reject Muhammad's messengership, demand a portent, dispute concerning Allah, and deny some of the revelation. They face torment in the life of the world and a more painful doom in the Hereafter, with the Fire as their reward.
Angels guard people before and behind them by Allah's command. They hymn Allah's praise with awe of Him and enter the heavenly Home through every gate.
The thunder hymns Allah's praise, and Allah launches thunderbolts and smites with them whom He wills while they dispute concerning Him.

l: the real prayer, Surah 13: The Thunder (Ar-Ra'd)
s: The real prayer belongs to Allah. Those prayed to beside Allah do not respond, and the prayer of disbelievers goes astray.

l: those who answered Allah's call, Surah 13: The Thunder (Ar-Ra'd)
s: Those who answered Allah's call have bliss. They are promised the heavenly Home and Gardens of Eden.

l: those who answered not His call, Surah 13: The Thunder (Ar-Ra'd)
s: Those who answered not Allah's call would offer all that is in the earth and its like as ransom, but they will have a woeful reckoning and hell as their habitation.
Hell is the dire abode and habitation of those who do not answer Allah's call.

l: men of understanding, Surah 13: The Thunder (Ar-Ra'd)
s: Men of understanding heed that what is revealed to Muhammad from his Lord is the truth. They keep Allah's pact, unite what Allah commands joined, persevere, pray, spend, and overcome evil with good.

l: the pact of Allah, Surah 13: The Thunder (Ar-Ra'd)
s: The pact of Allah is kept by those who heed the truth, and it is broken by those who ratify it and then sever what Allah commands joined.

l: the heavenly Home, Surah 13: The Thunder (Ar-Ra'd)
s: The heavenly Home is the sequel for those who persevere, pray, spend, and overcome evil with good. Those who break Allah's covenant have an ill abode instead.

l: Gardens of Eden, Surah 13: The Thunder (Ar-Ra'd)
s: Gardens of Eden are entered by the righteous and by those who do right among their fathers, helpmeets, and seed. Angels enter to them from every gate and greet them with peace.
Believers know that what is revealed to Muhammad from his Lord is the truth. They find rest in the remembrance of Allah and receive joy and a good journey's end when they do right.

l: the life of the world, Surah 13: The Thunder (Ar-Ra'd)
s: The life of the world is a brief comfort compared with the Hereafter. Those who disbelieve may rejoice in it, but torment also reaches them in it.
The Hereafter has a more painful doom for those who disbelieve than the torment of the life of the world. The reward of those who keep their duty is contrasted with the Fire.

l: the remembrance of Allah, Surah 13: The Thunder (Ar-Ra'd)
s: The remembrance of Allah gives rest to the hearts of those who have believed.
Allah guides unto Himself all who turn unto Him and sends whom He wills astray. Those whom Allah sends astray have no guide.
Messengers were sent before Muhammad and were mocked by those who disbelieved. Allah appointed wives and offspring for them, and no messenger could bring a portent except by Allah's leave.

The revelation is from Muhammad's Lord and is the truth, and it is revealed as a decisive utterance in Arabic. Muhammad is commanded to recite it to a nation whose members disbelieve in the Beneficent.
The text challenges disbelief in being raised after becoming dust and refers to a new creation. It also says that if a Lecture could make the dead speak, this Qur'an would have done so.
Punishment has occurred before among those who disbelieved, and Allah is strong in punishment. The disbelievers face torment in the life of the world and a more painful doom in the Hereafter.

l: the meeting with your Lord, Surah 13: The Thunder (Ar-Ra'd)
s: Allah details the revelations so that people may be certain of the meeting with their Lord.
Those who answer not Allah's call have a woeful reckoning. Allah's is the reckoning, and He is swift at reckoning.
Allah is the Creator of all things, and no partners can create like His creation. The text presents the creation of the heavens, earth, living things, rain, and celestial bodies as signs.
Prayer belongs truly to Allah, while prayer directed to others does not receive a response. Those who are righteous are regular in prayer and are promised reward.
Faith is associated with recognizing the revelation as truth, remembering Allah, finding rest of heart, and doing right. Those who disbelieve reject Muhammad and face punishment.

The unit concerns Allah’s revelation of Scripture through a messenger to bring mankind from darkness to light and guide them to the way of Allah. It recounts Moses’ call to his people, the rejection of messengers by earlier peoples, the fate of disbelievers in Hell, and the reward of believers in the Gardens. It presents Allah’s signs in the heavens and the earth, Abraham’s prayers concerning worship, his descendants, and the holy House, and warnings about the Day of Judgment. It concludes that the clear message teaches that Allah is One and calls people of understanding to take heed.

Allah reveals Scripture, guides and sends astray whom He will, and is the Creator and Owner of what is in the heavens and the earth. He promises increase to those who give thanks, destroys wrong-doers, rewards believers, and will repay every soul for what it has earned.
Scripture is revealed to a messenger so that mankind may be brought from darkness to light, by the permission of Allah, unto the path of the Mighty, the Owner of Praise.

Mankind is called to leave darkness for light, heed the warnings, worship Allah, and reflect on His signs. Mankind is also warned of the day when the doom will come and wrong-doers will seek reprieve.

The believers are told to put their trust in Allah, establish worship, and spend from what they have been given. Those who believe and do good works enter Gardens where they abide by permission of Allah.

The disbelievers prefer the life of the world to the Hereafter, debar others from the way of Allah, and are described as far astray. Their works are likened to ashes blown away by the wind, and they face Hell and a painful doom.
The Hereafter is preferred over the life of the world by those who follow the way of Allah. Allah confirms believers in the Hereafter and warns that the disbelievers face punishment there.

l: the way of Allah, Surah 14: Abraham (Ibrahim)
s: The way of Allah is the path to which Scripture brings mankind. The disbelievers debar people from it and would have it crooked.
The heavens belong to Allah, who created them with truth and can remove mankind and bring forth a new creation. On the final day, the heavens will be changed and people will come forth unto Allah.
The earth belongs to Allah, who created it with truth and provides its water and fruits. On the final day, the earth will be changed to other than the earth.
An awful doom awaits the disbelievers who reject Allah and turn people away from His way.
A messenger is sent with the language of his folk so that the message may be made clear to them. Messengers call people to Allah, but some people reject them and demand a clear warrant.

Moses is sent with Allah’s revelations to bring his people from darkness to light and remind them of the days of Allah. He reminds them of Allah’s favor in delivering them from Pharaoh’s folk and calls them to trust and give thanks.
Hell is before the froward potentate and contains festering water that is difficult to swallow. The guilty are exposed to it, and those who exchanged Allah’s grace for thanklessness are led to it.
Satan says that Allah promised a true promise while he promised and failed. He admits that he had no power except to call people, that they obeyed him, and that they must blame themselves.
The Gardens are entered by those who believe and do good works. Rivers flow beneath them, they abide there by permission of Allah, and their greeting is Peace.
A goodly saying is likened to a goodly tree whose root is firm and whose branches reach into heaven. It gives its fruit at every season by permission of its Lord.
A goodly tree has a firm root, branches reaching into heaven, and fruit at every season by permission of its Lord.
Worship is to be established by believers and is the purpose Abraham seeks for himself and some of his posterity. Abraham asks Allah to preserve him and his sons from serving idols.

l: the heavens and the earth, Surah 14: Abraham (Ibrahim)
s: The heavens and the earth are created by Allah with truth, and Allah causes water to descend and produces fruits for mankind. He also makes the ships, rivers, sun, moon, night, and day serviceable to mankind.

Abraham asks Allah to make his territory safe, preserve him and his sons from serving idols, and incline hearts toward his posterity. He asks for provision for them, the establishment of worship, forgiveness, and acceptance of his prayer.
The holy House is near the uncultivable valley where Abraham settles some of his posterity so that they may establish proper worship.
The uncultivable valley is near the holy House, where Abraham settles some of his posterity. He asks Allah to provide its people with fruits so that they may be thankful.

l: the Day of Judgment, Surah 14: Abraham (Ibrahim)
s: The Day of Judgment is a day when the guilty will come forth in chains, their raiment of pitch and the Fire covering their faces. Wrong-doers will ask for reprieve, but Allah will repay each soul for what it has earned.
A clear message is given for mankind so that they may be warned, know that Allah is only One Allah, and take heed as people of understanding.
Revelation is given to Moses and is sent through messengers to make Allah’s message clear to their peoples. It brings mankind from darkness to light by the permission of Allah.

This unit concerns Allah’s signs, commandments, mercy, and punishments, including the Night Journey of His servant from the Inviolable Place of Worship to the Far distant place of worship. It recounts what happened to Moses, the Children of Israel, Iblis, and mankind, and describes guidance, worship, resurrection, the Hereafter, reward, and hell. It teaches believers to worship Allah alone, honor parents, protect life and wealth, keep covenants, avoid adultery and wrongdoing, and speak kindly. It presents the Qur'an as guidance, healing, and mercy, and declares that Truth has come while falsehood is bound to vanish.

Allah carries His servant by night, reveals the Qur'an, guides whom He wills, provides for mankind, and knows and sees His slaves. He commands worship of Him alone, shows mercy, and appoints reward and punishment.

Muhammad is carried by night from the Inviolable Place of Worship to the Far distant place of worship. He is instructed to recite the Qur'an, convey warning and good tidings, speak kindly, establish worship, and call people to Allah.

Moses is given the Scripture as guidance for the Children of Israel and receives nine clear tokens. Pharaoh calls him bewitched, but Moses declares that the tokens were sent by the Lord of the heavens and the earth.

Iblis refuses to prostrate before Adam because Adam was created from clay. He asks for respite until the Day of Resurrection and vows to seize most of Adam’s seed, but Allah says he has no power over faithful bondmen.

l: Children of Israel, Surah 17: The Night Journey (Al-Israa)
s: The Children of Israel are given guidance and warned that they will work corruption in the earth twice. They receive power, wealth, and children, but punishment comes when they repeat corruption.

Mankind is honored, carried on land and sea, and provided with good things. Mankind is also described as hasty, thankless, grudging, and prone to disbelief, while each person is accountable for his own conduct.
Believers who do good works are promised a great reward. The Qur'an is described as healing and mercy for them.
Disbelievers reject the Qur'an, demand signs, and deny resurrection. Hell is appointed as their dungeon and painful doom.
The devil sows discord among people, is an open foe to mankind, and promises only to deceive. He is associated with squanderers, who are called his brothers.

l: Inviolable Place of Worship, Surah 17: The Night Journey (Al-Israa)
s: The Inviolable Place of Worship is the starting place from which Allah carries His servant by night.

l: Far distant place of worship, Surah 17: The Night Journey (Al-Israa)
s: The Far distant place of worship is the destination of the Night Journey, and its neighbourhood is described as blessed.
The earth is described as praising Allah together with the heavens and all things in it. Mankind is warned that it cannot rend the earth or reach the height of the hills.
The heaven is among Allah’s creation and praises Him with the earth and all things therein. The disbelievers demand that heaven fall upon them or that Muhammad ascend into it.
Hell is appointed as a dungeon for disbelievers and as the payment of those who follow Iblis. Its flame is increased whenever it abates for those who disbelieve Allah’s revelations.

The Qur'an guides to what is straightest and gives good tidings to believers who do good works. It is a healing and mercy for believers, a warning to wrongdoers, and cannot be matched by mankind and the jinn.
The Hereafter is the future state in which people are resurrected, summoned with their records, and judged. It is greater in degrees and preferment than the hastening life of this world.

l: Night Journey, Surah 17: The Night Journey (Al-Israa)
s: The Night Journey concerns Allah’s carrying His servant by night from the Inviolable Place of Worship to the Far distant place of worship so that He may show him of His tokens.
Revelation is sent by Allah to Muhammad and is divided for recitation to mankind at intervals. Allah states that what He reveals is by His mercy and that He can withdraw it if He wills.

Resurrection is described as the raising of people after they become bones and fragments. On the Day of Resurrection, people are summoned with their records and given their books in their right or other hands.

Worship is to be established from the going down of the sun until the dark of night, with Qur'an recited at dawn. People are commanded to worship none save Allah and to call upon Him with His beautiful names.
Guidance is provided by the Scripture and the Qur'an, which guides to the straightest way. Whoever follows guidance does so for the good of his own soul.
Allah’s mercy is hoped for by those who seek nearness to Him and is shown in His provision and revelation. People are instructed to ask for mercy for their parents.
Punishment comes upon those who corrupt, disbelieve, follow Iblis, or reject Allah’s revelations. Allah threatens repeated punishment if wrongdoing is repeated and describes punishment in hell.

The unit forbids killing children, adultery, wrongful killing, misuse of orphan wealth, dishonest measuring, following what one does not know, and exultant walking. It calls the killing of children a great sin.

Wealth is to be given in due measure to kinsmen, the needy, and the wayfarer, without wanton squandering. The wealth of an orphan must not be approached except in the better manner until the orphan reaches strength.
Truth has come and is declared to have prevailed. The Qur'an is sent down with truth and descended with truth.
Falsehood has vanished away and is bound to vanish. Those who follow it are described as astray and unable to find a road.
A great reward is promised to believers who do good works. Those who desire the Hereafter and strive for it as believers have efforts that find favor with their Lord.

This unit praises Allah for revealing the Scripture to Muhammad and warns believers and disbelievers about judgment, reward, and punishment. It recounts the People of the Cave, the two men and their gardens, and the meeting of Moses with the knowledgeable servant. It also tells of Dhu'l-Qarneyn, the people between the two mountains, and the barrier built against Gog and Magog. The unit emphasizes Allah's power, guidance, mercy, promise, and the limits of worldly life.

Allah revealed the Scripture to His slave, guides whom He wills, and alone has true protection, judgment, power, and worship. He rewards believers, punishes wrongdoing and disbelief, shows mercy, and knows the unseen, including the duration of the People of the Cave's stay.
Muhammad is addressed as the recipient of the revealed Scripture and is told to warn, recite, restrain himself with those who remember Allah, and proclaim that Allah is One.
The Scripture was revealed by Allah to His slave. It contains warnings, promises, accounts, similitudes, and guidance, and none can change Allah's words.
The believers do good works and receive the news of a fair reward, enduring gardens, and Paradise. They are encouraged to remain with those who call upon Allah and seek His Countenance.
The disbelievers reject Allah's revelations, dispute the truth, mock the revelations and messengers, and face hell, punishment, and loss of the value of their works.

l: the People of the Cave, Surah 18: The Cave (Al-Kahf)
s: The People of the Cave were young men who believed in their Lord and sought refuge in the Cave. Allah sealed their hearing, preserved them for years, awakened them, and disclosed them as a sign that His promise and the Hour are true.
The Cave sheltered the young believers, while Allah caused the sun to move away from them and caused them to turn over while asleep. They remained there for three hundred years and add nine.
The Hour is certain and there is no doubt concerning it. The unit warns that people may deny it and teaches that Allah will gather creation for it.
Paradise is described as the Gardens of Paradise prepared as a welcome for those who believe and do good works. They will abide there without wishing to leave.
Hell is prepared for disbelievers and is presented plainly to them. Its punishment includes fire, molten-like water, and a calamitous resting-place.

l: the life of the world, Surah 18: The Cave (Al-Kahf)
s: The life of the world is compared to vegetation made dry and scattered by the wind. Its wealth and children are an ornament, while enduring good deeds are better with Allah.

l: the two gardens, Surah 18: The Cave (Al-Kahf)
s: The two gardens belonged to one of the two men and contained grapes, date-palms, tillage, abundant fruit, and a river. They were destroyed after their owner was warned, leaving him regretful.

l: the two men, Surah 18: The Cave (Al-Kahf)
s: The two men are presented in a similitude about wealth, gardens, belief, and pride. One boasted of greater wealth and doubted the Hour, while the other rebuked him and affirmed Allah's oneness.

l: the garden owner's comrade, Surah 18: The Cave (Al-Kahf)
s: The garden owner's comrade reminded him that Allah created him from dust, a drop, and then as a man. He urged him to acknowledge Allah's power and later witnessed the destruction of the garden.

Moses traveled with his servant seeking the meeting point of the two rivers and later followed the knowledgeable servant to learn. He repeatedly questioned actions he could not understand and was told that he could not bear with them patiently.
Moses's servant accompanied him on the journey and forgot the fish at the rock, attributing the forgetfulness to Satan. He later informed Moses that the fish had taken its way into the waters.

l: the knowledgeable servant, Surah 18: The Cave (Al-Kahf)
s: The knowledgeable servant had received mercy and knowledge from Allah. He damaged a ship, slew a lad, and repaired a wall, then explained that each act served a hidden purpose ordained by Allah.
The ship belonged to poor people working on the river. The knowledgeable servant damaged it because a king behind them was taking every ship by force.
The king behind the poor people was taking every ship by force. His threat was the reason the ship was damaged.

The lad was slain by the knowledgeable servant because his future rebellion and disbelief were feared for his believing parents. Allah intended to replace him with one better in purity and nearer to mercy.

l: the two orphan boys, Surah 18: The Cave (Al-Kahf)
s: The two orphan boys owned the wall and the treasure beneath it. Their righteous father and Allah's mercy protected the treasure until they reached full strength.
The wall belonged to the two orphan boys and was near collapse. The knowledgeable servant repaired it without taking payment so that the treasure beneath it would remain protected.

Dhu'l-Qarneyn was made strong in the land and given a road to every thing. He traveled to the setting-place and rising-place of the sun and then to the region between the two mountains, acting with justice and building a barrier against Gog and Magog.

l: Gog and Magog, Surah 18: The Cave (Al-Kahf)
s: Gog and Magog were spoiling the land and could not surmount or pierce the barrier built against them. The barrier will be laid low when Allah's promise comes to pass.

l: the people between the two mountains, Surah 18: The Cave (Al-Kahf)
s: The people between the two mountains could scarcely understand speech and asked Dhu'l-Qarneyn to build a barrier against Gog and Magog. He accepted their assistance with strength instead of their tribute.

l: the two mountains, Surah 18: The Cave (Al-Kahf)
s: The two mountains marked the place where Dhu'l-Qarneyn found the people threatened by Gog and Magog. He leveled the gap between them with iron and molten copper to form the barrier.
The barrier was built from pieces of iron and molten copper between the two mountains. Gog and Magog could neither climb over it nor pierce it, but it will be laid low when Allah's promise arrives.
Iblis was of the jinn and rebelled against Allah's command when he refused to fall prostrate before Adam. He and his seed are presented as enemies who should not be chosen as protecting friends.
The angels were commanded to fall prostrate before Adam, and they did so except for Iblis.
Adam was the one before whom the angels were commanded to fall prostrate. His creation is referenced as part of the account of Iblis's rebellion.

l: the partners of Allah, Surah 18: The Cave (Al-Kahf)
s: The partners of Allah are false objects of worship that cannot hear prayers or help their claimants. Those who invoke them will find a gulf of doom between themselves and their supposed partners.
The messengers were sent as bearers of good news and warners. Disbelievers disputed with falsehood and mocked the revelations and what the messengers warned them about.

l: the revelations of Allah, Surah 18: The Cave (Al-Kahf)
s: The revelations of Allah provide guidance, warnings, similitudes, and reminders. Some people turn away from them, forget what they have sent forward, or treat them as a jest.

l: the Day of Resurrection, Surah 18: The Cave (Al-Kahf)
s: On the Day of Resurrection, people will be gathered, their deeds will confront them, and the works of disbelievers will receive no weight. The believers who do good works will receive Paradise.
The Judgment includes the placing of the Book, the exposure of every deed, and the punishment or reward of people. Allah does not wrong anyone.

l: the Words of Allah, Surah 18: The Cave (Al-Kahf)
s: The Words of Allah cannot be changed. Even if the sea became ink, it would be exhausted before the Words of Allah were exhausted.
Guidance comes from Allah, and the one whom Allah guides is rightly led. People who turn away from the revelations or follow their own lust may not be led aright.

Allah's mercy is sought by the young men of the Cave and is given to the knowledgeable servant. It is also shown in the protection of the orphan boys' treasure and in Allah's patience toward wrongdoers.

l: the promise of Allah, Surah 18: The Cave (Al-Kahf)
s: The promise of Allah is true, including the promise of the Hour and the final events involving the barrier. The People of the Cave were disclosed so that people would know that the promise is true.

This unit concerns Allah's mercy, commands, and judgments, especially as shown through Zachariah, John, Mary, Jesus, Abraham, Moses, Ishmael, and Idris. It recounts the births, missions, worship, and conduct of John and Jesus, and describes the guidance and trials of earlier prophets. It warns the disbelievers of resurrection, punishment, hell, and the Day of anguish, while promising the believers and righteous the Garden and Allah's love. It affirms that Allah has no son, that all beings belong to Him, and that all will return to Him.

Allah is the Lord of the heavens and the earth and all that is between them. He creates, guides, shows mercy, commands worship, raises the dead, gathers people for judgment, rewards the righteous, and punishes the disbelievers.

Zachariah secretly cries to Allah, asking for a successor because his wife is barren and he fears for his kinsfolk after him. Allah gives him the tidings of John and makes his sign that he will not speak to mankind for three nights despite having no bodily defect.
John is given his name, wisdom as a child, compassion, purity, and devotion. He is dutiful toward his parents and is described as neither arrogant nor rebellious.
Mary withdraws from her people to a chamber and receives the Spirit in the likeness of a perfect man. She conceives Jesus, gives birth in hardship, and returns to her people carrying him.
Abraham is described as a saint and a prophet. He urges his father to abandon powerless gods and serve Allah, withdraws from his people and their worship, and is then given Isaac and Jacob.

Muhammad is addressed as the one who warns people of the Day of anguish and other promised events. His tongue is made suitable for the Scripture so that he may give good tidings to those who ward off evil and warn the froward.

The disbelievers reject Allah's revelations, dispute the believers' position, and claim that the Beneficent has taken a son. They face punishment, hell, confusion by devils, and the gathering before Allah.
The believers are contrasted with those who disbelieve and are associated with better guidance and lasting good works. Those who believe and do good works receive love from the Beneficent.
The righteous are gathered as a goodly company unto the Beneficent. They are rescued from hell and inherit the Garden.
The heavens are nearly torn apart by the claim that the Beneficent has taken a son. They belong to Allah and all come unto Him as slaves.
The earth is described as nearly split asunder by the claim that the Beneficent has taken a son. Allah inherits it and all who are upon it.
Hell is where the guilty are driven and where the stubbornly rebellious are identified as most worthy to be burned. The evil-doers remain crouching there, while those who kept from evil are rescued.
The Garden is promised by the Beneficent to His slaves in the unseen. Its people hear no idle talk, receive peace and food morning and evening, and it is inherited by the devout.
The Scripture recounts the accounts of prophets and commands remembrance of them. It is made easy in Muhammad's tongue so that he may give good tidings and warnings.
The revelations of the Beneficent cause the prophets' descendants and chosen servants to fall down adoring and weeping. The disbelievers reject the clear revelations.
Worship includes prayer, almsgiving, service to Allah, and steadfastness in His service. Later generations ruin worship and follow lusts, while the prophets and righteous uphold it.

Allah's mercy is shown to Zachariah, Mary, Jesus, Abraham, and other prophets and servants. The Garden is promised through the mercy of the Beneficent, and Jesus is described as a mercy from Allah for mankind.

l: the Day of Resurrection, Surah 19: Mary (Maryam)
s: On the Day of Resurrection, each person comes to Allah alone. The righteous are gathered to the Beneficent, while the guilty are driven to hell.

l: the Day of anguish, Surah 19: Mary (Maryam)
s: The Day of anguish is the day when the case has been decided. People are warned because they are presently careless and do not believe.
The Hour is among the events promised to those in error. When they behold it or its punishment, they will know who is worse in position and weaker as an army.
The text describes a day when the case is decided, people are gathered before Allah, and each one comes to Him alone. The righteous are rewarded and the guilty are punished.

This unit concerns the revelation of the Qur'an to Muhammad and Allah's commands, guidance, and warnings. It recounts Moses' mission to Pharaoh, the signs given to Moses, the contest with Pharaoh's magicians, and the deliverance of the Children of Israel through the sea. It describes the Children of Israel's trial with As-Samiri and the calf, and Moses' response. It also presents teachings about Adam, Iblis, the Garden, guidance, resurrection, the Day of Judgment, hell, and the Hereafter.
The Qur'an is revealed as a reminder, in Arabic, containing threats and lessons so that people may avoid evil and take heed. Muhammad is told not to hasten with it before its revelation is perfected.
Muhammad receives the Qur'an and is told to bear patiently with what people say, praise Allah, and ask for increased knowledge.

Allah is described as the only deity, the Creator, the Beneficent, the True King, and the One who knows what is hidden and apparent. Allah guides, forgives, provides, judges, and rewards or punishes people according to their deeds.
The Hour is surely coming, but Allah keeps its time hidden so that every soul may be rewarded for what it strives to achieve.

Moses is chosen, addressed by Allah, given signs, and sent with Aaron to Pharaoh. He asks for ease, eloquence, and Aaron's help, confronts Pharaoh's magicians, leads the Children of Israel away by night, and returns angrily when they worship the calf.
Moses' staff is used for leaning, tending sheep, and other purposes. When he casts it down, it becomes a serpent, and Allah commands him to take it without fear.

Pharaoh is described as having transgressed and as leading his people astray. He challenges Moses, threatens Moses' followers and the magicians, pursues the Children of Israel, and is covered by the sea with his hosts.
Aaron is appointed to share Moses' task and strengthen him. He warns the Children of Israel against the calf, but they refuse to stop worshipping it until Moses returns.
The Children of Israel are delivered from Pharaoh, given a covenant, and provided manna and quails. In Moses' absence, many are misled by As-Samiri into worshipping the calf.
Pharaoh's magicians make their cords and staves appear to run by their magic. They accept defeat, believe in the Lord of Aaron and Moses, and refuse to prefer Pharaoh over the clear proofs.

Magic makes the cords and staves appear to move, but Moses' sign consumes what the magicians have made. The magicians confess that Allah is better and more lasting, and Pharaoh threatens them for believing.
As-Samiri misleads the Children of Israel during Moses' absence and produces the calf from the ornaments. Moses condemns him and declares that he will have a tryst he cannot break.

The calf is made of a saffron hue and gives forth a lowing sound. The Children of Israel call it their god, but it cannot return a saying or possess harm or benefit; Moses burns it and scatters its dust over the sea.
Allah commands Moses to make a dry path through the sea for the Children of Israel. Pharaoh follows with his hosts, and the sea covers them.
Hell is the destination of whoever comes to his Lord guilty. There the guilty person neither dies nor lives.
Gardens of Eden, beneath which rivers flow, are prepared for believers who do good works. They remain there forever as the reward of those who grow.
The text describes people being brought forth again and assembled after the Trumpet is blown. The guilty are gathered in terror, and the mountains are reduced to scattered dust.
Adam receives a covenant but forgets and lacks constancy. He eats from the forbidden tree, then is chosen, forgiven, and guided by his Lord.
Iblis refuses Allah's command to prostrate before Adam. He is identified as an enemy of Adam and his wife.
The angels are commanded to prostrate before Adam, and all do so except Iblis.
The Garden is a place where Adam and his wife do not hunger, become naked, thirst, or suffer the sun's heat. They are sent down from it after eating from the tree.
The devil whispers to Adam and presents the tree of immortality and power that does not waste away. His whisper leads Adam and his wife to eat from the tree and become aware of their shame.
Allah promises that whoever follows His guidance will not go astray or come to grief. Guidance is connected with following revelation and walking aright.
Moses is commanded to serve Allah and establish worship for His remembrance. Muhammad is told to enjoin worship upon his people and remain constant in it.
Allah commands Moses and Aaron not to be faint in His remembrance. Muhammad is told to glorify Allah at various times, and turning away from remembrance is linked to a narrow life.
Faith is shown by the magicians who believe in the Lord of Aaron and Moses and by those who come to Allah as believers. Believers who do good works receive high stations and fear no injustice.
Good works accompany belief and lead to high stations and the Gardens of Eden. Allah does not diminish the reward of those who do good works.

Punishment is threatened for those who lie against Allah, deny revelation, turn away, or come to their Lord guilty. Pharaoh threatens punishment, while Allah's punishment includes hell and the burden borne on the Day of Resurrection.
Revelation comes from Allah and includes the Qur'an, the commands given to Moses, and the guidance sent to people. It is presented as a reminder, warning, and proof.
The Hereafter is described as more severe and lasting for those who reject Allah's revelations. It includes reward in the Gardens of Eden and punishment in hell.

l: the Day of Judgment, Surah 20: Taa-Haa
s: On the Day of Judgment, the Trumpet is blown, the guilty are assembled, intercession benefits only by Allah's permission, and faces humble themselves before the Living, the Eternal. Those who turn away from remembrance are brought blind and face the consequences of their deeds.

Surah 21 concerns the approaching reckoning of mankind, the oneness of Allah, and the rejection of idolatry. It recounts how Allah supported messengers and prophets including Abraham, Lot, Moses, Aaron, Noah, David, Solomon, Job, Dhu'n-Nun, and Zachariah, while destroying wrong-doing peoples. It describes revelation, resurrection, the balance of justice, punishment in hell, and mercy for the righteous and believers. Muhammad is sent as a mercy for the peoples and warns that Allah is One.

l: Surah 21: The Prophets (Al-Anbiyaa), Surah 21: The Prophets (Al-Anbiyaa)
s: It presents warnings about the approaching reckoning, the oneness of Allah, the fate of wrong-doers, and the mercy shown to believers and the righteous.
Allah is the One Lord, Creator and Sustainer of the heavens and the earth. He sends revelation, supports His messengers, judges justly, punishes wrong-doers, and shows mercy to the righteous.
Muhammad is warned that mankind's reckoning is near and is mocked by those who disbelieve. He is sent as a mercy for the peoples and instructed to proclaim that Allah is One.
Mankind's reckoning draws near while many turn away heedlessly. Mankind is made of haste and every soul must taste death.
The wrong-doers reject the message, mock messengers, and ask for portents. They are threatened with punishment and destruction.
The disbelievers deny revelation, mock Muhammad, and question the promised punishment. They will face fire that comes upon them unexpectedly.
The messengers before Muhammad were men who received inspiration. They were mocked, but what their mockers ridiculed eventually surrounded the mockers.
The prophets received inspiration and guided people by Allah's command. They established worship, performed good deeds, and gave alms.
